title: Should Teachers Show Examples of Their Own Work to Students
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to a question from art teacher Emily Stuver about whether teachers should show students their own creative work, Stuart argues emphatically yes, but only under specific cultural conditions. He distinguishes between peer-to-peer comparison, which he considers far more damaging to student motivation and specifically the Belonging belief, than student-to-teacher comparison, since students rarely measure their self-worth against an adult's skill level. He argues the real prerequisite is building a classroom culture where a discipline is treated as an infinite game of personal improvement rather than a competition, and that within that culture, sharing your own work sends a powerful Credibility signal while modeling process supports the Effort and Efficacy beliefs. He gives practical guardrails: joke about experience gaps, frame your role as making clear the unclear, and work in short 3-4 minute visible bursts rather than lengthy demonstrations. The piece is a worked example of how Stuart applies his Five Key Beliefs framework to answer a specific pedagogical question from a colleague.
points: Distinguishes peer comparison from student-to-teacher comparison, arguing the former is far deadlier to student motivation and the real threat to Belonging, not a teacher's visible competence.
Prescribes a specific cultural precondition — treating the discipline as an infinite game of personal improvement versus a finite game of competition — before modeling work becomes safe to use.
Recommends showing process, not just product, in short 3-4 minute intervals so students see decision-making and struggle rather than a finished, intimidating piece.
Ties the technique explicitly to two of the Five Key Beliefs: sending a Credibility ooh ah wow signal, and clarifying the unclear to support Effort and Efficacy.
quotes: One side says only put up the examples that other students have done or just the mere basics so that students won't take one look at a project and give up because they can't fathom being able to compare to what they see.
Spoiler alert: I answer with an emphatic YES. However, certain conditions must be cultivated for this method not to backfire.

But when a student fancies themselves a student artist and then discerns at the completion of a project that their piece is inferior to many of their peers, this can be quite rattling. It can act just like a ravenous beast, devouring the student's sense of self as an artist.
The solution to this is crafting a class culture where art is an infinite game of personal improvement versus a finite game of competition.

It's very powerful to create work in front of students — not at length, as this can be boring, but for 3-4 minute intervals, talking through as you work the barriers you're having to overcome, the decisions you're making.

It sends an "ooh ah wow" signal of Credibility (the most foundational of the Five Key Beliefs). It makes clear the unclear (this is critical for the Effort and Efficacy beliefs, especially for secondary students).
